subtopic: Planning a wedding and family expectations
subtype: Approach: pausing to reset after a conflict over guests [Revision]
passage: Pradeep, you look tense about your guest list, so let me tell you what my husband and I did. I'm Shreya. Ten days before our wedding we had a shouting match over it. He wanted a hundred and fifty, and I had found myself adding relatives until it reached three hundred. I walked out to the balcony, he stayed in the kitchen, and we didn't speak for an hour. Then he came out with two cups of tea. We set a cap of two hundred and a rule: exceptions only if both of us agreed. The next day we sat with each set of parents and said why: "We want to be able to talk with everyone who comes." Both families listened. It hurt less because we had both stopped fighting first.

qa.q: What cap did the couple set for the guests?
qa.a: They set a cap of two hundred.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel on walking out to the balcony?
qa.a: Shreya was upset and frustrated after the shouting match, and needed a pause before speaking again.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped end the fight, and why?
qa.a: Stopping for an hour and then agreeing a cap with a rule for exceptions helped, because it replaced arguing about numbers with a shared limit.

qa.q: How might Shreya's husband have felt when he brought out the two cups of tea?
qa.a: He probably felt regret and a wish to make peace, offering tea as a way to reopen the conversation.

grounding: Illustrates a couple stepping back after a heated fight over the guest list, agreeing a cap and a rule for exceptions and explaining it kindly to both families.
